dek: Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery's megamerger now has one unified identity.

slides.label: What Happened
slides.text: Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison announced the combined company will be called *Skydance*.

slides.label: The Merger
slides.text: The $110 billion merger between Paramount and *Warner Bros. Discovery* is set to close next week.

slides.label: Legal Hurdle Cleared
slides.text: A judge approved Paramount's settlement with California and *11 other states* that sued over the deal.

slides.label: Film Commitment
slides.text: Paramount must release a minimum number of theatrical films over five years, starting with *30 films* a year.

slides.label: New Leadership
slides.text: Ynon Kreiz, former chairman and CEO of *Mattel*, has been named co-CEO of the newly combined company.

slides.label: Timeline
slides.text: The merger is expected to officially close on *October 6th*.

slides.label: Why It Matters
slides.text: For Black, Brown and Latino storytellers, the studio's film quotas and new scale could mean more shots at getting greenlit.

question: Will the Skydance merger open more doors for underrepresented filmmakers?

caption_instagram:
Hollywood just got a new name and it's bigger than you think.

Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery's $110 billion merger is closing next week, and the combined company will be called Skydance. CEO David Ellison says the name keeps both studios' legacies in the spotlight instead of burying them under a new corporate brand.

The deal also comes with real commitments: Paramount must release at least 30 theatrical films a year for the next two years, and former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz is stepping in as co-CEO.

Will the Skydance merger open more doors for underrepresented filmmakers?

caption_linkedin:
A $110 billion media merger just got its final name: Skydance.

Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery's combination closes next week, and CEO David Ellison chose the name specifically to avoid overshadowing either studio's brand equity, a smart move for an industry built on legacy IP.

The deal cleared its last legal hurdle this week after a judge approved a settlement with California and 11 other states. It also locks in a production commitment: at least 30 theatrical films annually for the first two years. Former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz joins as co-CEO, bringing fresh operational leadership to the newly scaled company.

For founders and operators watching the media landscape, this is a case study in brand strategy during consolidation, and in how production quotas can shape who actually gets greenlit.

Will this merger create more pipeline for underrepresented creators, or just consolidate power further?
